name: Fatima Baker

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We aren't linked to any AI company, employer, union or party. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Sure. I teach maths at Eastfield Academy, a big secondary school with about 1,400 kids, mostly ages eleven to sixteen. I'm in by half seven, photocopying is long gone because I build everything on the screen, and I usually teach five lessons out of six. The best bit is when a Year 9 who's decided they're 'not a maths person' suddenly gets algebra and goes a bit pink.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Marking and data, honestly. Every six weeks we enter grades into the tracker, and the meetings about the tracker take longer than the marking. I already use AI every day to draft worksheets and write differentiated questions, which has given me back maybe four hours a week. Daniel, my partner, is a physio, and he says I talk about spreadsheets more than he talks about knees.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: And money, how are things at home?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Pretty comfortable for my age. I'm on the upper end of the pay scale for my experience because I took on the Year 8 maths coordinator role, and Daniel and I rent a two-bed near the ring road. I've got about ten months of costs saved and a small index fund I add to every month. We're saving for a house deposit, no kids yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I already say in the staffroom: the tools are useful but they're not magic. I'd probably post something on the maths teachers' forum about which prompts actually work for writing practice questions. Honestly, I'd be the person telling the sceptics it's fine and telling the hype people to calm down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it means my job stays my job, which is fine by me. I'd keep my four hours a week from AI and carry on. If anything I'd be a little disappointed, because I'd hoped it would kill the marking pile properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep teaching, keep the coordinator role, and probably go for the head of maths job at Eastfield when Mrs Oduya retires in two years. I'd keep paying £300 a month into the index fund and put the rest toward the deposit. Maybe I'd write a short guide for the department on using AI for practice questions, because people keep asking me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. A bit flat, like when a film everyone talked about turns out to be just okay. My work and money feel steady, so there's not much to worry about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said a bit disappointed. What exactly did you hope AI would take off your plate?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The Friday marking. I sit in the kitchen with 90 exercise books and a cup of tea going cold. If an AI could mark the books and tell me which six kids didn't get fractions, I'd spend Friday evenings with Daniel instead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If nothing much changes, what's the biggest pressure left in your life?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: House prices, not robots. Every flat we like near Daniel's clinic goes up by more than we save in a year. The real enemy for my generation is the deposit, and AI hype doesn't touch that.

say: I'd say AI is **useful but not magic**, and share which prompts actually help with practice questions.
I'd tell sceptics it's fine and tell the **hype crowd** to calm down.
think: Privately I'm relieved my **job stays mine**, though a bit disappointed it didn't fix marking.
My real pressure is the **house deposit**, not AI.
do: Apply for **head of maths** when Mrs Oduya retires in about two years.
Keep paying **£300 a month** into the index fund and saving for a deposit.
Write a short **AI guide** for the maths department.
feel: Mostly **calm**, with a flat, slightly let-down feeling.
S0.quote: If an AI could mark the books and tell me which six kids didn't get fractions, I'd spend Friday evenings with Daniel instead.
fieldNote: Fatima already uses AI daily and saves about **four hours a week**, so a plateau barely moves her.
Her main worry is **housing costs**, which she says AI hype doesn't touch.
She frames ambition through promotion: the **head of maths** post is her next step.

steps.text: Apply for head of maths at Eastfield when the post opens
Keep paying £300 a month into the index fund
Write a short AI practice-question guide for the maths department

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say teachers who learn the tools will be fine and the ones who refuse will have a rough few years. I'd volunteer to run the training at Eastfield, because someone's going to and I'd rather it's someone who teaches. Online I'd probably post examples of AI marking going wrong next to examples of it going right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think it's mostly good for me. The thinking tasks in my job are planning, marking, writing reports and answering parent emails, and if AI takes those, I get more time in the room with kids. The risk is the trust deciding fewer teachers can cover more classes with AI tutors, and maths is exactly the subject they'd try that with.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd do the trust's AI lead course, the one they keep advertising, and try to become the person who sets up AI marking for the department. I'd keep saving and keep the index fund going, and I'd look at a part-time master's in education technology in the evenings, maybe £4,000 a year. If Eastfield started cutting maths posts, there are four other secondaries within half an hour, so I'd move.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited, and a little guilty about being excited. I can picture older colleagues like Mr Pearce really struggling, and I don't want to be smug about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My colleague Mr Pearce has taught maths for thirty years and still prints everything. He's brilliant with the difficult Year 11 group, but he'd hate being told to check what a computer wrote. I'd worry the school sees him as slow when he's actually the one the kids listen to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said maths is the subject they'd try fewer teachers with. Does that sit with feeling excited?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fair point, it doesn't fully. I think I'd be one of the teachers who survives the cut, partly because I'm young, cheap-ish and good with the tools. My job is probably safe, but the department could easily lose two posts, and I'd feel that.

say: I'd say teachers who **learn the tools** will be fine and refusers will struggle.
I'd offer to **run the training** at Eastfield so a teacher leads it.
think: AI taking **planning and marking** gives me more time with kids, which I'd love.
The trust might cut **maths posts** and use AI tutors, though I'd likely survive.
do: Take the trust's **AI lead course** and set up AI marking in the department.
Start a part-time **master's** in education technology, around **£4,000 a year**.
Move to one of **four nearby secondaries** if Eastfield cuts maths posts.
feel: **Excited**, with some guilt about colleagues who'll struggle.

fieldNote: She sees Steady Disruption as **mostly good** for her own job and income.

steps.text: Take the trust's AI lead course and set up AI marking

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In public I'd say kids still need a person in the room, and that's true. I'd probably push the union and the trust to be honest about what happens to teaching jobs, because there'd be a lot of rumours. Online I'd try to be the calm voice, not the doom voice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, two years is very fast for a school. AI that can explain maths better than me, at any hour, for every kid, is basically the main thing I'm paid for. I think schools keep teachers for supervision, safety and behaviour, but the pay and the number of posts could drop a lot, and a maths specialist premium might disappear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Straight away I'd stop the house hunt and keep the deposit as cash, because I wouldn't want a big mortgage on a job I'm unsure of. I'd push to be the person at Eastfield who designs how the AI tutors run, since someone has to plan the timetable and the safeguarding. I'd also look hard at pastoral roles, like head of year, because looking after kids is the hands-on bit robots don't touch until around 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. It's a fizzy kind of anxious, because part of me wants to be in the middle of it. But I can't picture what a maths teacher earns in 2029, and that's unsettling.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you and Daniel talk about that first night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Whether we still buy the house. Daniel's job is physio, hands-on, so he'd have until about 2031 before robots matter, maybe longer. I'd say we keep renting, keep the cash, and let his job be the steady one for a while, which would be a strange flip for us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned pastoral roles. Is that a real plan or a hope?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit of both. I'm good with the kids who are struggling, and Mrs Oduya has already asked if I'd mentor a tutor group. If teaching maths becomes mostly the AI, I'd rather be the person who knows why a kid hasn't eaten breakfast than the person who checks the AI's algebra.

say: I'd say kids still need a **person in the room**.
I'd press the **union and trust** to be honest about teaching jobs.
think: AI that explains maths better than me covers the **main thing** I'm paid for.
Schools keep teachers for supervision, but **posts and pay** could drop a lot.
do: **Pause the house hunt** and keep the deposit as cash.
Bid to **design how AI tutors** run at Eastfield, including safeguarding.
Move toward a **pastoral role** like head of year.
feel: **Anxious**, with an eager edge because she wants to be involved.
Unsettled that she **can't picture** a maths teacher's pay in 2029.
S2.quote: If teaching maths becomes mostly the AI, I'd rather be the person who knows why a kid hasn't eaten breakfast than the person who checks the AI's algebra.
fieldNote: She treats the thinking AI date as the real threat; her own teaching is mostly **explaining**, which AI can do.
She'd lean on Daniel's **hands-on job** as the steadier income for a while.
Her plan B is **pastoral care**, the part robots reach later and AI can't easily replace.

steps.text: Pause the house hunt and keep the deposit as cash
Volunteer to design how AI tutors run at Eastfield
Apply to become head of year or a pastoral lead

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got five years, so let's not waste them, and I'd mean it. I'd want Eastfield to write a proper plan for what teachers do in 2031, not just a policy on cheating. I'd be loud about it in meetings, which my head of department would find either useful or annoying.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, five years is enough time for me to land somewhere good. I'd be 32 when it arrives, with savings and some experience leading things. The people I'd worry about are the ones who wait until year four.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I'd finish the master's faster, maybe full-time evenings for two years, and take on the trust's AI lead role. By year three I'd want to be either head of year or working at the trust office designing how AI tutoring works across six schools. We'd probably still buy a smaller flat, but with a shorter mortgage and a bigger deposit, so the payments fit on Daniel's wage alone if needed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy but quite purposeful. Five years feels like a runway rather than a cliff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you cut back to fund the faster master's?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Holidays first, which hurts because we love Portugal. Probably also the second car we keep talking about. I'd still keep the index fund going, even if it's only £100 a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd buy a flat sized for Daniel's wage alone. That sounds more worried than 'purposeful'.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, that's the honest part. My job probably changes rather than disappears, but I'd want the house safe even if my pay drops by a third. Planning for the bad version lets me feel purposeful about the rest.

Buy a **smaller flat** whose mortgage fits Daniel's wage alone.

S3.quote: My job probably changes rather than disappears, but I'd want the house safe even if my pay drops by a third.
fieldNote: Five years turns her mood from anxious to **purposeful**; she plans careers, not escape.

steps.text: Finish the education technology master's within two years
Take the trust's AI lead role across six schools
Buy a smaller flat with a mortgage Daniel's wage covers
Drop holidays and the planned second car

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty if schools start now, and I'd mean schools, not just teachers. I'd probably post that the worst thing a school could do is assume it's someone else's problem. At work I'd ask for a ten-year staffing plan, which nobody has ever written.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, ten years takes me to 37, which is when I'd want to be a deputy head anyway. Deputy heads spend their days on people, parents and behaviour, and that work lasts longer than explaining equations. So the long version mostly lines up with where I was heading.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my plan: head of maths in two years, then assistant head, using AI tools all the way. I'd do the master's at a normal pace and not panic-buy anything. Daniel and I would buy the house in the next year or two, and I'd overpay the mortgage so it's small by 2036.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly calm, with something in the back of my mind. I've got time, money and the right skills, but I'd still watch the maths department numbers every September.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you change any family plans?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe we'd have kids a bit sooner, around 30, so they're older and I'm more settled before things change. That sounds odd, but I'd rather be on maternity leave in 2029 than in 2035. My partner Daniel would laugh at me planning a baby around AGI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you watch for, each September?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: How many maths teachers we hire and how many AI licences we buy. If one goes down while the other goes up for two years running, I'd start moving faster. I like having a clear signal.

I'd ask Eastfield for a **ten-year staffing plan**.

Buy the house soon and **overpay the mortgage** before 2036.
Have **kids around 30** so they're older when things change.
feel: Mostly **calm**, with a watchful thought at the back of her mind.
S4.quote: I'd rather be on maternity leave in 2029 than in 2035. My partner Daniel would laugh at me planning a baby around AGI.
fieldNote: Even calm and well placed, she'd **check hiring** every September for warning signs.

Buy a house within two years and overpay the mortgage

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, easily. Two years isn't enough for a school to work out what teachers are for, and the people in charge would grab the cheapest answer. What would help is a clear national rule on how many adults must be in a classroom, plus paid time to retrain while we still have our jobs.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the kids. I'm fine, honestly, but my Year 11s are going to leave school into whatever this is. I'd love someone to tell me what to teach a sixteen-year-old in 2028, because I genuinely don't know.

headlineQuote: I'd love someone to tell me what to teach a sixteen-year-old in 2028, because I genuinely don't know.
portrait: Fatima is a **27-year-old maths teacher** at Eastfield Academy who uses AI every day.
She has **ten months saved**, an index fund and a physio partner, Daniel, and is saving for a house.
She's calm about slow change and sees AI freeing her from **marking**.
AGI by 2028 makes her **anxious**: she'd pause the house hunt and move toward pastoral work.
With more warning she keeps her **promotion path** and even plans children around it.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because schools would grab the cheapest answer before working out what teachers are for.
whatWouldHelp: A national rule on **adults per classroom** and paid **retraining** time while teachers still have jobs.
